title: The landlord must return the security deposit when you move out
law: Indian Contract Act, 1872, s.73; your rent agreement
plain: A security deposit is your money held against unpaid rent or damage. When you move out, the landlord may keep only what is shown to be owed (unpaid rent, bills, damage beyond normal wear and tear) and must return the rest. Refusing to return it without a reason is a breach of the agreement, and you can claim the amount plus compensation for loss caused by the breach.

title: Model Tenancy Act: deposit cap and refund on vacating (only where a state has adopted it)
law: Model Tenancy Act, 2021, s.11 (as adopted by a state)
plain: Under the Model Tenancy Act, a residential deposit can be at most two months' rent, and the landlord must refund it when the tenant hands back the house, after lawful deductions. It applies only in states that have passed a law based on it, and those states have a Rent Authority where you can apply. Elsewhere your state's Rent Control Act and the agreement apply.

title: Send a legal notice before going to court
law: General practice (a notice is not compulsory against a private person, but courts and commissions expect one)
plain: A legal notice is a formal letter that states what happened, what you want (for example the deposit amount) and a deadline, usually 15 days. Send it by Speed Post or Registered Post with acknowledgement and keep the receipt and tracking printout. Many disputes end here, because the other side now sees you are serious.

title: Recover the money in a civil court; summary suit if there is a written agreement
law: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXVII; Limitation Act, 1963 (3 years for money claims)
plain: If the notice does not work, you can file a civil suit for recovery of money in the court that covers where the property is or where the other side lives. Where the claim is on a written contract (like a signed rent agreement), a faster 'summary suit' under Order XXXVII is possible. Money claims generally must be filed within 3 years.

title: You are a consumer and can complain about defective goods or poor service
law: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.2(7), s.2(10), s.2(11), s.2(47)
plain: Anyone who buys goods or pays for a service (including online) is a consumer. A defect in goods, a deficiency in service (late, poor or not delivered), or an unfair trade practice (for example refusing a promised refund) gives you the right to complain to a Consumer Commission.

title: Which Consumer Commission, and you can file where you live
law: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.34; Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021
plain: Claims up to Rs 50 lakh go to the District Consumer Commission, Rs 50 lakh to Rs 2 crore to the State Commission, and above Rs 2 crore to the National Commission. You can file in the district where you live or work, not only where the company is. You can file online on the e-Daakhil portal (edaakhil.nic.in) without a lawyer.

title: Time limit: 2 years
law: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.69
plain: A consumer complaint must be filed within 2 years from the day the problem happened (the cause of action). A delay can be excused only with a good reason.

title: No court fee for claims up to Rs 5 lakh
law: Consumer Protection (Consumer Commission Procedure) Regulations, 2020
plain: There is no fee for consumer complaints of up to Rs 5 lakh. Above that a small fee is charged on a slab basis.

title: Free first step: National Consumer Helpline 1915
law: Department of Consumer Affairs, National Consumer Helpline
plain: Before filing a case you can register a free grievance with the National Consumer Helpline: call 1915, use the NCH app, or consumerhelpline.gov.in. It forwards the complaint to the company, and many refunds are settled at this stage. Keep the docket number.

title: E-commerce sites must have a grievance officer who replies on time
law: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, rule 4(5)
plain: Every e-commerce platform must name a grievance officer, acknowledge a complaint within 48 hours and resolve it within one month. Write to that officer first and save the reply or the lack of one.

title: What the Commission can order
law: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.39
plain: The Commission can order the seller or service provider to refund the price, replace or repair, pay compensation for loss and harassment, and pay your case costs.

title: Wages must be paid on time, and within 2 working days after you leave
law: Code on Wages, 2019, s.17 (in force from 21 November 2025)
plain: Monthly wages must be paid by the 7th day of the next month. If you resign, are removed or are laid off, all wages due must be paid within two working days. Holding back earned salary, or making deductions not allowed by law, is not permitted.

title: File a wage claim with the Labour Department
law: Code on Wages, 2019, s.45
plain: You can file a claim for unpaid wages before the authority appointed by the Labour Department in your area. It can order the employer to pay the wages and extra compensation. Filing is cheap and needs no lawyer. The claim must be filed within 3 years.

title: Conciliation through the Labour Commissioner
law: Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (conciliation)
plain: You can also complain to the office of the Labour Commissioner, which calls both sides for a conciliation meeting. Bring your offer letter, salary slips, bank statements and messages about the unpaid salary.

title: A bounced cheque for a debt is a criminal offence
law: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, s.138
plain: If a cheque given to pay a debt is returned unpaid because of insufficient funds (or 'exceeds arrangement'), the person who signed it commits an offence, punishable with up to 2 years in jail and/or a fine of up to twice the cheque amount. The cheque must have been presented within its validity (3 months from its date).

title: Send the demand notice within 30 days of the bank's return memo
law: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, s.138(b) and (c)
plain: You must send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of getting the bank's 'cheque return memo'. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving the notice to pay. Missing the 30-day window loses the criminal case, so this deadline matters most.

title: File the complaint within 1 month after the 15 days end
law: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, s.142
plain: If the drawer does not pay within the 15 days, file a complaint before the Magistrate within one month. The case goes to the court where your bank branch (where you deposited the cheque) is located.

title: Interim compensation of up to 20%
law: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, s.143A
plain: While the case is going on, the court can order the drawer to pay you up to 20% of the cheque amount as interim compensation.

title: A legal notice is a letter, not a court order
law: General law (a notice starts a dispute; only a court can order you to do something)
plain: A legal notice is a demand letter from the other side or their lawyer. It is not a judgment and does not mean you have been sued. You do not commit a crime by not replying, but a short, calm reply that denies wrong claims protects you later. Do not admit anything you do not agree with, and do not pay in panic.

title: A court summons is different: never ignore it
law: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order V; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
plain: If the paper is a summons from a court (it has a case number, court name and a date to appear), you must appear or send a lawyer on that date, or the court can decide against you. Free legal aid is available for this.

title: How to reply to a notice
law: General practice
plain: Reply in writing within the time mentioned (often 15 days), by Speed Post or Registered Post, and keep proof. Answer each claim, state your side with dates, attach nothing original (only copies), and say that you reserve your rights. Check whether the notice is about money, property or a cheque, because cheque notices (Negotiable Instruments Act s.138) have strict timelines.

title: Report online fraud immediately: call 1930
law: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs
plain: Call the cyber fraud helpline 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in as fast as possible. If reported within the first hours, the money can often be frozen in the receiving account before it is withdrawn. Note the transaction ID, UPI ID or account number, time and amount.

title: Tell your bank within 3 working days for zero liability
law: RBI circular on customer liability in unauthorised electronic transactions, 6 July 2017
plain: If money left your account without your authorisation because of a fraud by someone else, and you inform your bank within 3 working days, your liability is zero. Reporting in 4 to 7 working days limits your loss to a capped amount. The bank must credit the amount (shadow reversal) within 10 working days of your report and resolve the complaint within 90 days. If you shared an OTP or PIN yourself, the bank may hold you liable until you report it.

title: The fraud is a crime: FIR or e-FIR
law: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s.318 (cheating); Information Technology Act, 2000, s.66C and s.66D; BNSS, 2023, s.173 (Zero FIR)
plain: Online cheating is a crime under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the IT Act. You can file an FIR at any police station (a 'Zero FIR' is registered even if the fraud happened elsewhere) or through the cybercrime portal. Ask for a copy of the FIR or complaint acknowledgement; banks ask for it.

title: RBI Ombudsman if the bank does not help
law: Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021
plain: If your bank or payment app rejects your complaint or does not reply within 30 days, complain free of cost to the RBI Ombudsman at cms.rbi.org.in.

title: Free legal aid from the Legal Services Authority
law: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, s.12
plain: Women, children, Scheduled Castes and Tribes, industrial workers, persons with disabilities, people in custody, victims of disasters and people below an income limit set by the state get a free lawyer. Contact the District Legal Services Authority at your district court or call NALSA's helpline 15100.

title: Lok Adalat: free settlement, final decision
law: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, s.19-21
plain: A Lok Adalat settles disputes by agreement, even before a case is filed (pre-litigation). There is no fee, and its award is final and binding like a court decree. Ask the District Legal Services Authority for the next Lok Adalat date.

title: Keep proof
law: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (electronic records are evidence)
plain: Screenshots of chats, emails, bank statements, receipts, agreements and call logs are valid evidence. Keep the originals safe, make copies, and note the date of each message. Do not delete chats with the other side.

title: Emergency helplines
law: Government helplines
plain: Police, ambulance, fire: 112. Women in distress: 181. Children: 1098. Mental health support (Tele-MANAS): 14416. NALSA legal aid: 15100.

title: Domestic violence: protection orders
law: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
plain: A woman facing physical, emotional, sexual or economic abuse at home can approach the Protection Officer or the Magistrate for protection, residence and maintenance orders. Call 181 or 112 if in danger. Free legal aid is available.
